terms.comment: From male and facere, the one who does wrong. The adjective, criminal, wicked, is maleficus, malefica, maleficum.
Frequent as a noun, chiefly in the plural, sontēs (Lewis & Short); see guilty.

terms.gloss: criminal, villainous; as a noun, a criminal
terms.comment: Rare but classical; Cicero uses the plural as a noun (Cat. 2.22, Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: wicked; as a noun, a villain, a scoundrel
terms.comment: Common in comedy as a term of abuse, sceleste!; Cicero does not use it of persons (Lewis & Short).
Traupman’s word for criminals, but classically ‘reproachful, slanderous’ (Cic., Liv.); ‘a guilty man’ only in Cassiodorus (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: neque ego hōc homine quemquam vīdī magis malum et maleficum
phrases.english: and I have never seen anyone more wicked or more of a villain than this man
they shall keep the prisons for criminals

phrases.latin: ego hunc scelestum in jūs rapiam exulem
phrases.english: I’ll drag this villain into court, the outcast!
